Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.

"We both bear responsibility for the ⁠international order ​and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.

President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.

"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.

Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.

The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.

On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.

Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz said.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference  "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

#1059. Troy Parrott dreaming of home Euros as Ireland boost seeding with Nations League win

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Republic of Ireland 3-0 Kosovo: Parrott’s brace ensured Ireland will be in pot two for the qualifying draw as they co-host the 2028 tournament

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Troy Parrott is daring to dream of playing in a home European Championship after helping lift the Republic of Ireland to a 3-0 Nations League victory over 10-man Kosovo.

The Real Betis striker contributed two penalties on Tuesday night at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, where Jack Moylan added a late cushion to ensure the Republic secured a coveted seeding spot in pot two for next month’s Euro 2028 draw.

Finishing runners-up in group B3 also assured them of a place in the Nations League League A/B playoffs, with one of Denmark, Wales, Croatia or Serbia awaiting them in March.

“I’ve been thinking about it since I was a kid, I think everyone has,” Parrott, asked about the 2028 championship, told RTÉ.

“Look, it’s not a guarantee that we are going to qualify for that tournament, so I think tonight was very important to get into pot two so that we have a better draw.

“We’ll be going into the qualifiers now trying to make sure that we qualify for the tournament.

“A tournament that’s one of the host nations being Ireland, without Ireland it would be heartbreaking for all of us, so I think it’s a mission now to make sure that we’re there.”

The 24-year-old was delighted to come out on top after what he branded a series of “nearly games”, including a 2-2 draw with group winners Austria at the Aviva Stadium last month and Saturday’s 1-0 loss in Linz.

The Republic were gifted an advantage in the 26th minute on Tuesday night, when Kreshnik Hajrizi was sent off for handling the ball off the line.

Parrott, who added his second penalty five minutes after the restart before Moylan put the game away with 15 minutes remaining, said: “It was disappointing that we didn’t win the group because that’s what we all wanted to do at the start.

“There’s been so many nearly matches where we’ve nearly won, we’ve played really well and haven’t won, and I think tonight we went out there with the mindset that no matter what we have to win.

“Obviously the red card helped us, but I have no doubt in my mind that group of players who were out on that pitch would have won that game.”

Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson brushed aside suggestions that his players should fear a Nations League promotion, insisting they all want to go up.

He said: “Everybody, and especially us, likes to play the top teams. To compare yourself with the best teams, that’s one thing.

“Second is those teams will expose your weaknesses, and that helps you in your growth, to play these teams, so we can continue our growth.

“We’re already looking forward to March. Tough teams in the pot. Whoever we draw is going to be a tough two games, and it’s good for this team at this time to play these matches instead of friendlies.

“We’re really excited for March, and looking forward to meeting the players again.”

Representatives of Manchester City's first-team squad are reportedly positioning themselves to move their clients on, should the club be hit with severe sanctions

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Representatives for multiple Manchester City first-team players are exploring whether their clients could leave the club on free transfers if City fail in all legal appeals against the Premier League, according to a new report.

Investigative journalist and former Times reporter Nick Harris has claimed that Real Madrid president Florentino Perez is 'increasingly confident' of signing striker Erling Haaland ahead of next season.

Harris wrote on Twitter/X: “Florentino Perez [is] increasingly confident Erling Haaland will be a Real Madrid player next season according to a contact who had lunch with Perez recently. Meanwhile multiple MCFC players' agents [are] exploring how their players might leave on free transfers if all City appeals fail. IF.”

Harris’s emphasis on the word 'if' reflects that any potential departures remain conditional on the final outcome of City’s long-running regulatory dispute with the Premier League.

The club were charged in February 2023 with more than 100 alleged breaches of the league's financial regulations spanning nine seasons between 2009 and 2018, alongside allegations of failing to cooperate with the subsequent investigation.

An independent commission began hearing the case in late 2024, with any initial ruling subject to an appeals process that both the Premier League and the club have the right to pursue.

Manchester City have consistently denied all wrongdoing since the charges were announced, maintaining that their position is supported by a comprehensive body of evidence.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Despite the club's public stance, agents representing members of Enzo Maresca’s squad are reportedly conducting legal due diligence to assess their clients' contractual options should severe sporting sanctions be imposed and upheld once all avenues of appeal are exhausted.

Under FIFA’s Regulations on the Status and Transfer of Players (RSTP), a footballer may apply to terminate a contract without sporting or financial penalty if they can establish 'just cause.' In sports employment law, significant disciplinary penalties against a club - such as expulsion from the top flight, relegation, or a prolonged exclusion from UEFA competitions - can be argued to fundamentally alter the terms under which a player signed their agreement.

If such claims to be upheld by football's governing bodies, affected players would in theory become free agents, enabling rival clubs to sign them without paying Manchester City a transfer fee. Like most clubs, the Cityzens' financial operating model relies on player trading and maintaining high squad valuations to comply with UEFA and the Premier League's Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) legislation. Therefore, losing senior assets for free would make for a major financial headache.

Real Madrid will be among the clubs closely monitoring legal developments in Manchester. Perez has long viewed Haaland as a transfer target, and according to Harris’s source who dined with the Madrid president recently, the Spanish club anticipate an opportunity to bring the Norway international to the Santiago Bernabeu ahead of the 2027/28 campaign.

Haaland signed a statement nine-and-a-half-year contract extension with Man City in January 2025, committing his future to the club until 2034. Under normal market conditions, buying the striker out of that agreement would require a world-record transfer fee, meaning any realistic prospect of a move to Madrid in the short term is closely tied to how Man City’s legal proceedings conclude.

No formal transfer requests or contractual termination mechanisms can be triggered while the disciplinary process and any subsequent appeals remain unresolved. However, the initial legal inquiries allegedly being carried out by intermediaries indicate that agents are actively preparing contingency plans ahead of a final verdict.

#1057. Former Manchester United midfielder Juan Mata announces retirement from football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Spaniard won the World Cup, European Championship and major honours with Chelsea and Manchester United

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Juan Mata, the former Chelsea and Manchester United playmaker, announced his retirement at the age of 38 on Wednesday, concluding a storied international and club career.

A key part of Spain's most successful era in international football, Mata finished with 41 appearances and 10 goals. He lifted the World Cup in South Africa in 2010 and scored in the final of Euro 2012 two years later.

"Sometimes, to love is to let go... Thank you, football," Mata captioned a video on his Instagram.

The midfielder was widely praised for his technical ability and deft touch. In 2017, he co-launched the charity Common Goal, an initiative encouraging footballers to pledge one percent of their income to fund community projects and drive social change.

After starting out in Real Madrid's youth system, Mata emerged at Valencia before moving to Chelsea in 2011, where he won the Champions League, FA Cup and Europa League before departing for United in 2014.

During his time with the Red Devils, Mata won the Europa league, FA Cup and League cup before leaving the Premier League after a decade at the top level.

Leaving in 2022, Mata secured league titles in Turkey with Galatasaray and Japan with Vissel Kobe before wrapping up his career in Australia.

Mata left Melbourne Victory in September following a final season that produced five goals and 12 assists in 25 appearances.

Manchester United are a ridiculous mix of previous eras: they should be competing already, yet they're starting all over again from scratch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Albert Einstein never did say that thing about insanity. There's no proof of it, anyway. Researchers have looked, and in fact, it likely comes from a 12-step recovery pamphlet from the 1980s that it might not be wise to expect a different result from doing the same thing over and over again. That makes a little more sense all-round.

Michael Carrick can attest. So can Ruben Amorim and Erik ten Hag, with all three likely to be watching Mauricio Pochettino from a podcast studio near you in the coming months, like the hologram ghosts of Yoda, Obi-Wan and Anakin.

It's a theme of Ratcliffe's Nice regime, too. The Ligue 1 side were fitted with a revolving door upon their INEOS takeover, with seven separate managers named as permanent boss since Patrick Vieira's dismissal in lockdown – including Christophe Galtier, Lucien Favre, Franck Haise and Claude Puel. Nothing stuck. Ross Barkley spent nine months at the Allianz Riviera before leaving by mutual agreement. Kasper Schmeichel spent 13 months before terminating his own deal. Aaron Ramsey didn't make it to a full year before doing the same. Last season, gravity took over, Les Aiglons finishing 16th and having to enter the relegation play-off in order to secure top-tier status. It's not dissimilar to Old Trafford. Perhaps the ownership simply needs to stick at something a little longer, rather than taking the approach of a toddler burning through a box of toys until they've exhausted everything at their fingertips. Manchester United have no idea what they're supposed to be. It's plainly obvious. They had very little semblance of identity under Ten Hag, yet extended his contract anyway: they sacked him mere months later and went down the continental route of hiring a back-three manager who very obviously didn't have the squad for what he wanted to do (but should have done far better with what he had).

So United wedded themselves to Amorim. They brought in a wing-back in Patrick Dorgu. They improved the frontline with two wingers who would stay narrow and a target man to play off of them. They had half the squad that the Portuguese wanted, but things weren't going well enough. They sacked him and brought in Carrick, a manager who brought a feel-good factor, excelled in big games when he didn't have to be the protagonist, but lacked the control to play his football.So United wedded themselves to Carrick. They brought in Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos as more Carrick-type midfielders and listened to him when he said he wanted to trust Marcus Rashford. We're not even into post-bugle November, and the manager's gone, replaced by a priest of the high press. Manchester United don't have a particularly mobile midfield. That frontline doesn't exactly look like the type to celebrate tackles. One would like to believe that perhaps the powers that be have seen something in Pochettino's United States team that can be replicated in English football once again. Previous evidence perhaps suggests otherwise.

One would like to believe that United have seen something in Pochettino that can be replicated. Previous evidence perhaps suggests otherwise.

The quote was wrong. Insanity is pivoting in wildly different directions every few months, expecting to surge up the table. United have been left a Ship of Theseus (or Trigger's Broom, the Sugababes or Frankenstein's monster, depending on your age and culture). A dressing room made up of passers Ten Hag believed in playing out the back with, hero-ball counter-attackers for a back three and a couple of midfielders that reminded Carrick of himself. There's a defender still there that Jose Mourinho believed in, one that Ole Gunnar Solksjaer wanted to build around and even one that Louis van Gaal thought was the future. This is a squad of discarded parts, all pulling in different directions: and we're meant to be surprised when one erupts and goes rogue in an interview?Are you building a football club or a reality TV show cast, here? With all the respect in the world to the players themselves, it's frankly ridiculous that none of them have anything in common besides the badge on their chest. Mikel Arteta took about three and a half years to get Arsenal competing for titles, because he had to weed out those who weren't aligned with his thinking. INEOS have been in English football about that long: they've beaten the champions to signings in that time, but they're starting the process all over again.

Maybe we can lay all of the fault at the feet of Ratcliffe, a man who proves on the regular that he's out of touch with the very fanbase he claims to be among, and who has previously operated the very same business model across the channel to staggeringly meh results. Maybe it's Jason Wilcox or Omar Berrada, who have apparent carte blanche to keep digging until they find hope at the bottom of the chest. Maybe it's the fault of that bloke who's not cutting his hair, putting pressure on the lads. Maybe United really do have too many dinnerladies, and it's led to a culture of stagnation at Carrington. Maybe the cabal of former United legends – sponsored by Betway or Midnite or Huel – don't exactly help matters when they tell us all how things weren't like this in their day, and how United just miss the gaffer. None of them, for what it's worth, know what Manchester United should look like. Even Gary Neville has said that the identity under Sir Alex Ferguson was to be adaptable: have the ball some weeks, cede it others. But even Neville knew in his management career that chopping and changing was deadly. “I didn't know what to do with the players; I was changing systems,” he's admitted of his Valencia stint. “All the things that I say on television now you should never do, and it was too much.”Sometimes, doing the same thing over and over again isn't insanity at all. If United don't even have consistency in their decision-making, how on Earth are they going to find it on the pitch?

#1055. Kozo Tashima submits Fifa presidential bid to signify rupture in Asia’s backing of Gianni Infantino

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

JFA honorary president Tashima officially submitted his candidacy for the Fifa presidency after securing the support of five national federations

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president Kozo Tashima has officially submitted his candidacy for the Fifa presidency after securing the support of five national federations, signifying a rupture in Asia’s backing of Gianni Infantino.

Nominations for the Fifa presidential election close at 10:59pm GMT on Wednesday, four months before the 77th Fifa Congress in Rabat on 18 March, where the vote ⁠will take place.

Infantino is seeking re-election for a fourth term as head of global football’s ruling body, with any challenging candidates needing at least five member associations to nominate them.

They should also have played an active role in football for two of the last five years as a player or official within Fifa, a confederation or a national association.

Tashima is a former Japan international ⁠and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for Fifa president. He ​has ⁠served on the Fifa Council since 2015.

“The JFA submitted to Fifa a letter nominating me as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election," Tashima said in a statement shared by the JFA.

"I would like to once again express my gratitude to President (Tsuneyasu) Miyamoto and all the members of the board. I would also like to sincerely thank the football associations of many countries who gave me the necessary support for this nomination.

"With a strong sense of mission ‌and determination, I will take on this challenge so that Fifa can become a healthier and more trusted organization and contribute to the further development of football around the world."

He did not disclose which associations' nominations he had received, but told reporters at the Asian Football Confederation's (AFC) annual awards ceremony in Thailand on Wednesday he would later reveal which nations had backed him.

Asked about his ‌objectives, the 68-year-old said: "First and foremost, I believe it is essential to establish proper governance and ensure that transparency is firmly maintained.

"We must get that right first. Then, on top of that, various policies can be put forward."

Candidates must pass formal eligibility and integrity checks before standing for election, and Fifa’s general secretariat must notify member associations of the proposed candidates for president at least one ⁠month before the Congress.

Infantino has faced opposition to his re-election over his aborted attempt to bring private investors into a new Fifa commercial entity holding rights linked to competitions including the World Cup.

The Swiss later apologised to the Fifa Council for the way the proposal had been handled.

Other challengers include former Switzerland captain Ramon Vega and French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo.

Tashima said he was aware that he was "not necessarily in an advantageous position" heading into the election.

"From here, I need to think carefully about what strategy to adopt, what kind of manifesto to create, and how to make my case," he added.

Diallo, who was drafted in at the last minute as European governing body Uefa’s candidate, said at a press conference on Tuesday he would reach out to Tashima to "unite our forces".

Tashima said he had not yet spoken with Diallo.

"I have spoken indirectly with people around him, but we have not discussed specifically what we would do," he added. "Mr. Diallo only recently made his announcement, so I would like to speak with ‌him at least once going forward."

Asia's regional confederation ⁠had already said it was backing Infantino before Tashima announced his intention to run earlier this month.

AFC head Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa publicly endorsed the Swiss administrator at their extraordinary congress in Tokyo in October, just two months after describing his plan to sell a stake in Fifa tournaments as a "breach of trust".

Asked about ‌his position once again on Wednesday, Sheikh Salman ​told reporters: "Well, we already made our stance.

"We mentioned that, whether it's during the AFC Executive Committee meeting in Vancouver (in April), or during the congress in Tokyo. It's as simple as that.

“I prefer that you talk to the member association more, hear it from them."

#1054. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1051. Kai Havertz should have been awarded penalty against Hull, KMI panel finds

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The panel also backed penalty decisions involving Coventry and Everton, while agreeing Manchester United’s late equaliser against Aston Villa was correctly allowed to stand.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

An independent panel has unanimously ruled that Arsenal were incorrectly denied a penalty against Hull for a foul on Kai Havertz while the German was in an offside position.

The attacker was held back by Nobel Mendy at the Emirates Stadium on November 7, but referee Farai Hallam gave nothing on the pitch. VAR Michael Oliver recommended Hallam review the incident, yet no spot-kick was awarded due to Havertz being offside.

The five-person Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel unanimously determined that a penalty should have been given both on field and following review based on the chronology of events.

The panel established that Mendy’s holding occurred prior to any potential offside offence by Havertz. Law 11 states that a player in an offside position when the ball is played by a teammate is only penalised upon becoming involved in active play.

The panel also unanimously disagreed with the decision not to award Coventry a penalty against Everton on November 6 when James Tarkowski pulled the hair of Caleb Yirenkyi.

It concluded that the incident ought to have been penalised with a spot-kick and a yellow card shown to Tarkowski.

There was unanimous agreement with the decision to allow Manchester United’s equaliser in their 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on November 8 to stand.

Replays indicated United goalkeeper Senne Lammens may have impeded opposite number Zion Suzuki when challenging for the ball, but the panel was satisfied that the contact lacked impact and remained below the threshold for a foul.

The panel was divided over a challenge by Leeds’ Jayden Bogle on Tottenham’s Mathys Tel on November 7. Two members felt referee John Brooks should have shown Bogle a red card and that VAR Tony Harrington ought to have intervened, but three felt that while the contact was clearly reckless, it fell below the threshold for a red card, backing the on-field decision and the non-intervention.

Across the 10 match rounds so far, 223 KMIs have been assessed, with 85 per cent of on-field decisions deemed correct, rising to 97 per cent following VAR intervention.

Scotland will hope those absences prove costly for Switzerland in a game they have to win, while also hoping North Macedonia — who are yet to pick up a point in Group B1 — take points off Slovenia.

Sebastien Pocognoli claimed his first home victory on Friday against the North Macedonians, thanks to John McGinn's second-half double. The Scots will need to produce their best performance under the Belgian manager if they are to triumph in St Gallen, though.

Scotland have no new injury concerns, but captain Andy Robertson is set to become his country's record appearance-maker. The Tottenham Hotspur defender should win his 103rd cap tonight, taking him past the legendary Sir Kenny Dalglish.

The absence of key players should weaken the hosts, opening the door for Scotland to get a result — but maybe not the result they want.

#1049. Man United want Mauricio Pochettino to turn them into Tottenham – it won’t be easy

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

As Pochettino takes the Old Trafford job, there are a slew of obstacles that will prevent him from immediately turning Man United into his Spurs side of a decade ago

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Officially, Manchester United have appointed the USA manager Mauricio Pochettino. The hope at Old Trafford may be that they have actually appointed Tottenham Hotspur manager Mauricio Pochettino.

The Argentinian has had higher-profile jobs since, one (PSG) that yielded silverware, another that put him in charge of a host nation at a World Cup, but for many his defining work remains at White Hart Lane. It earned him admirers in Manchester, Sir Alex Ferguson and Gary Neville among them. As the man who seemed the great lost United manager finally arrives at Old Trafford, part of the aim is simply to replicate what he did in north London.

Pochettino played attacking, energetic football, galvanised the crowd and united them behind the club, improved players, turned signings into successful buys, prospered with a limited budget, mounted a title challenge, qualified for the Champions League on a regular basis and reached a Champions League final. United would appreciate it if he did all that again. If they are greedy, they may ask him to win the Premier League and bring in other silverware. From the depths of the relegation zone, however, they should not get ahead of themselves.

And making United Tottenham 2.0 comes with certain complications. If one of them is that Pochettino is now 54, and there is a school of thought United should have appointed him a decade ago when he was 44 and when Louis van Gaal left, another lies in the group he has inherited. Pochettino’s Spurs were relentless runners. Michael Carrick’s United ranked 19th for distance covered this season – ahead only of Sunday’s opponents, Liverpool – and whereas the Argentinian is indelibly associated with pressing football, his new captain Bruno Fernandes complained after the defeat to Como about the lack of pressing. Yet much of this team feels ill-equipped to press frenetically or adopt a high defensive line.

That is not entirely their fault. On average, Pochettino’s Tottenham were the youngest team in the Premier League in each of his first three seasons in charge. Now United are one of the older sides.

The manager is not alone in offering evidence of the passing of time. He is reunited at Old Trafford with Luke Shaw: a teenager at Southampton, an injury-prone thirty-something now. The Argentinian’s Tottenham team were notable for quick, dynamic full-backs, Danny Rose and Kyle Walker in particular. Shaw once met that description: now he, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui scarcely do. Patrick Dorgu has the pace and dynamism, but there are doubts if he is a full-back.

In the centre of defence, Pochettino’s preferred double act at Spurs was the Belgian axis of Toby Alderweireld and Jan Vertonghen; each furnished with positional intelligence, each excellent in possession and, if not electric, at least quick enough to defend on the halfway line. In contrast, Bournemouth’s third goal at Old Trafford illustrated that Harry Maguire is not, while Matthijs de Ligt isn’t either, explaining Carrick’s preference for a mid-block. Maguire and De Ligt are more of ball-playing defenders than Leny Yoro, who at least has the speed Pochettino can appreciate. A fondness for left-footed centre-backs suggests Lisandro Martinez could be pivotal, despite his dreadful season.

In midfield, United’s £150m summer overhaul scarcely seems designed with Pochettino in mind. Only one of their quartet has the required mobility and he, Carlos Baleba, is injured. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and the homegrown Kobbie Mainoo can tend to get outrun; Tielemans at least has age as a mitigating factor. But rewind to Pochettino’s first season at White Hart Lane and his flagship choices were Nabil Bentaleb and Ryan Mason; neither ultimately top class and each later displaced from the side, but young players who could set the tone with their running power. United do not have an obvious Bentaleb or Mason.

Most obviously, they do not have a Harry Kane either; in a recent interview, Erik ten Hag lamented their inability to buy the striker in 2023, without mentioning that United might have been able to afford the England captain had he not wasted £85m on Antony. Kane could represent Pochettino’s greatest success while, with Benjamin Sesko sidelined, United have no specialist striker available.

United can note the 2016-17 Spurs scored 86 league goals, at least 13 more than they have managed in any season since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. Kane was a huge factor in that, but not the only one. Heung-Min Son flourished as a goalscoring winger who could run in behind defences; perhaps only Bryan Mbeumo, if used wide, and Marcus Rashford might meet those criteria. A ‘what if?’ of Rashford’s career is if, were he managed by someone like Pochettino or Jurgen Klopp at a formative stage, would he press more effectively and enthusiastically?

So there may only be one encouraging precedent from Pochettino’s Tottenham. While he has often favoured 4-2-3-1, he usually played 3-4-2-1 in 2016-17, when his side earned 86 points. But whatever the formation, he often had two – some would say three, including Mousa Dembele – players with very different skillsets, but who could be called No 10s, including Dele Alli and Christian Eriksen, with the Dane often playing off the right.

Now United have Fernandes as the central creator plus Matheus Cunha, Mason Mount and Tielemans, who arguably all have designs on the role. That they were signed by four different managers and are now bequeathed to a fifth is an indication of the difficulties of Pochettino’s inheritance.

He managed to make sense of Spurs in a way few have done before or since. If, for much of the Premier League era, Tottenham may have looked on enviously and wondered how they could become United, now United may want to emulate the Spurs side of a decade ago. But a glimpse at Pochettino’s new charges shows it will not be easy.

#1048. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#1047. Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion and Italy's first since 1953 when he finished third in Sunday's thrilling and crash-hit Mexico City Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

#1046. Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 620–627 (2026) Cite this article

Corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets are central to climate action, but they often fall short of driving meaningful business transformation. Despite progress in standardization, current target-setting approaches remain weakened by methodological problems, including inaccurate emissions accounting, excluded emissions sources and limited comparability across companies. More importantly, many corporate targets are disconnected from the real-world sectoral transitions required to meet the Paris Agreement’s temperature goal. Drawing on evidence from four editions of the Corporate Climate Responsibility Monitor and recent literature, we argue that target-setting frameworks should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains. We propose transition targets as a practical complement to traditional greenhouse gas reduction targets. These targets would incentivize, guide and measure progress towards sector-specific milestones, such as electrification, low-carbon material uptake and the phase-out of emissions-intensive technologies. Embedding transition targets in accountability standards, and eventually in regulation, could help close the gap between corporate climate commitments and real-world action. It would also align corporate target-setting with the physical transition benchmarks introduced by the Paris Agreement’s Global Stocktake. The scientific community has a key role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

#1044. Mauricio Pochettino sends message to Man Utd fans ahead of first day: ‘Give me time’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino has arrived at Carrington after signing off his reign with the USA by beating Haiti on Tuesday night

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino said to “give him time” to make Manchester United the city’s dominant club again after taking charge of his last match in charge of the United States.

The US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati to wrap up an 8-0 aggregate victory in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final.

AC Milan forward Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with a spectacular overhead kick and teenager Julian Hall doubled the hosts’ lead before half-time.

Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time against Liverpool on Sunday after being appointed to succeed Michael Carrick, and arrived at the club’s Carrington training ground on Wednesday afternoon as he began work as their new head coach.

Pochettino, who has signed a deal until the summer of 2029, jetted into Manchester after the victory over Haiti and was whisked to the club’s training base to meet United staff and start preparations his first match.

His final message as USA manager was towards United fans, asking for patients as he looked to restore the footballing hierarchy in Manchester to what it used to be.

Told by former Manchester City loanee DaMarcus Beasley that “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue” in the TNT Sports studio after the game, Pochettino responded: “You will see. Give me time.

“The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it’s adrenalin you want to feel.

“We need to add our common sense… we know the situation is not a situation that deserves to be a club like Manchester United, the fan base is amazing.”

Pochettino heads to Old Trafford having led the US to the last 16 at this year’s World Cup on home soil.

“The mentality is to learn from everyone,” Pochettino told reporters. “You need to have an open mind because I think the players can teach us everyday, we are much better coaching staff now.

“Football is about attitude, and it’s about the approach. It’s about connection, feelings and communication.”

#1041. Has Uefa fumbled the chance to bring down Gianni Infantino as Fifa president?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Infantino was badly wounded after his disastrous attempt to sell of stakes in the World Cup and Club World Cup. But ahead of Fifa’s presidential election, his strength appears restored

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It has been nearly four months since journalists at The Times and Financial Times exposed Gianni Infantino’s shady plan to sell off 20 per cent of the World Cup and other Fifa tournaments to private investors, having sought approval from JP Morgan Chase, Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s brother, but almost no one inside Fifa and absolutely no one in the wider football world.

It sparked a humiliating chain of events for Infantino. His senior advisor resigned calling it “a bad deal for football”. His chief operating officer said Fifa colleagues had been “deceived”. Uefa threatened to boycott future World Cups unless the scheme was scrapped. National associations withdrew their support and continental federations united against him. Fifpro, the global players’ union, accused Infantino of a “profound abuse of power”.

The scathing attacks kept coming and in that moment it seemed hard to imagine how Infantino could possibly struggle on, let alone stand in spring’s presidential election.

Yet ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for election rivals to submit their candidacy, Infantino’s strength appears largely restored. He sacked his most vocal critic inside Fifa, COO Kevin Lamour. He went on a round-the-world tour visiting more than 30 countries in an effort to shore up support. He vowed to vastly increase per-nation spending from $1m to $25m by January, enough to convince the president of the Asian confederation, Sheikh Salman Al-Khalifa, to U-turn and throw his weight behind Infantino’s re-election.

In the background, Uefa has been scrabbling around for a rival candidate. Aleksander Ceferin decided to stay on as Uefa president rather than risk taking on Infantino and losing. Arsene Wenger, Fifa’s head of football development, weighed up a bid but decided against it. So, with about 48 hours to go, Uefa revealed their candidate to challenge Infantino was a Frenchman named [checks notes] Philippe Diallo.

What do we know about Diallo? He is a trained lawyer, career sports administrator and the current head of the French Football Federation. His father was a Senegalese boxer and there is hope inside Uefa that African roots might help sway a few votes. But in a game of personalities, he is a worryingly low-profile figure. This is a man whose entire Wikipedia entry contains fewer words than the section of Infantino’s page labelled ‘honours and awards’, where you will find a series of titles about as meaningful as the Fifa Peace Prize, including a Friendship Medal from Vladimir Putin.

There is still time for sentiments to change, but right now Infantino is the clear frontrunner. He needs 106 votes of the 211 national associations, and is thought to hold large swathes of support throughout Africa (54 votes), Asia (47) and South America (10). He may even retain support in quiet corners of Europe too. Uefa’s disorganised attempts to line up an eye-catching contender have only bolstered Infantino’s position.

There is some disappointment within Uefa that Wenger didn’t step forward, though in reality he has always been an Infantino loyalist. Wenger’s condemnation of the World Cup sell-off was alarmingly slow and indirect, and he has shown little appetite to bite the hand that feeds him.

There remains some confidence of overcoming Infantino among figures inside Uefa, although much of it stems not from their election hopes but across the Atlantic, where another election may have changed the picture. The Democrats’ success in the recent US mid-terms will bolster their numbers in the House of Representatives from January, and they could then issue subpoenas to lay bare Infantino’s relationship with Trump.

There is also Uefa’s concerted pursuit of documents which it hopes will reveal the gory details of the sell-off plan. A New York court rejected Fifa’s attempts to block the documents from being released, although they are still yet to emerge. Uefa hopes they may lead to a criminal trial.

Infantino’s opponents within Uefa feel one of these avenues could lead to his downfall. It will have to be seismic: there is already plenty to criticise about his reign as Fifa president, and almost nothing has so far eroded his power.

Infantino performatively began his presidency on an Easyjet flight, yet he quickly got a taste for the good life and nobody seems to mind that he now flies around in private jets. There was the absurdity of Trump’s peace prize, and the brazen sporting scandal that was Folarin Balogun’s lifted suspension. Yet, ultimately, Infantino has been very good at delivering promised money for federations, and that happens to be a useful vote-returning mechanism.

Infantino shouldn’t really be standing in this election, of course. Fifa presidents are only supposed to serve a maximum of three four-year terms, but he found a loophole and Fifa “clarified” just before the Qatar World Cup that his first three years didn’t count, rather he was finishing Sepp Blatter’s work. He could now lead until 2031, completing a 15-year reign, quite the stint for a man who declared in his very first speech: “The new Fifa is a democracy, not a dictatorship.”

If the legal routes fail to remove Infantino, he could still be voted out when the presidential election comes around in March. But it seems only one man will stand to challenge him. And if you’ve got to the end of this article and forgotten his name, then that is part the problem.

#1040. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

#1039. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#1038. Why Sunderland should be wary but not worried about their second-season syndrome

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Sunderland are candidates for the drop - but they don't need to panic just yet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Second-season syndrome. You’ve heard the cliché: a team enjoys a brilliant campaign immediately after promotion to the Premier League, only to endure a pronounced slump the following year. This time around, Sunderland are the afflicted side.

Many tipped the Black Cats to struggle this term despite finishing seventh on their top-flight return – their best league placing for a quarter of a century – and clinching European qualification for the first time since the 1970s. They did less transfer business in the latest window than most other Premier League clubs (though they were somewhat limited in what they could do having splashed the cash the previous summer) and there was a sense the added strain of Europa League football would take its toll. Head coach Regis Le Bris recently acknowledged as much, saying: “We are exposed this season with this busy schedule. Is it unexpected? I don’t think so.”

Granted, that was shortly before Sunderland went on to beat Chelsea 1-0 for just their second league win of the season, but the fact remains that Le Bris’ men sit second-bottom of the Premier League table after 10 games; they are, by all accounts, suffering from second-season syndrome.

In one sense, no – a lot of impressive newly promoted teams do have a dip the next season – but in another sense, absolutely, as far as the ultimate outcome of the phenomenon is concerned: most sides who experience second-season syndrome don’t end up getting relegated.

That’s only happened 11 times in the Premier League’s 34-year history – and never to Sunderland (who have been relegated in their first season back in the top flight on two occasions). It’s also only happened to two teams in the last 11 years: Huddersfield in 2019 and Sheffield United in 2021 – the former of whom had only dodged the drop by four points the previous campaign anyway (so was that even second-season syndrome?).

Besides, and perhaps tellingly in the end, Sunderland’s underlying numbers are not indicative of a side in severe danger of relegation.

They sit seventh in the Premier League’s expected points (xPTS) table, calculated using each team’s expected goals (xG) for and against (xGA). So far, their main issue has been taking their chances – as evidenced by their league-low tally of eight goals (three of which have been Enzo Le Fee penalties, including the winner against Chelsea last time out).

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Brian Brobbey showed with his hat-trick in September’s 5-3 defeat to Manchester City how clinical he can be – but, as much of a handful as the big Dutchman is and for all he offers as a highly physical attacking focal point, he hasn’t scored in any of his other seven Premier League outings this term.

It wouldn’t be an oversimplification, then, to say the solution to Sunderland’s problems is to sign a striker or two. The slight hitch is that the January transfer window is still six weeks away… Sunderland have eight Premier League games to play between now and then – plus two in Europe and a Carabao Cup quarter-final.

There is room for improvement defensively – Sunderland rank 15th in the Premier League for xGA (16.4) and have conceded almost exactly in line with that (16 goals) – but statistically, they are the eighth-best creators in the top flight, accumulating 15.6 xG – which just highlights how wasteful they have been in front of goal.

All in all, though, Sunderland shouldn’t be bricking themselves about the threat of relegation. Their major shortcoming is eminently fixable – through a combination of improved finishing (and it might only take one confidence-boosting win to spark their season into life, as Nottingham Forest, similarly creative but goal-shy, seem to have done by beating Manchester City 3-1 before the international break) and some smart January recruitment.

It might also benefit Sunderland (and their fans might not want to hear this) to go out of Europe early. Halfway through the Europa League league phase, they sit 11th – which would put them into a play-off to reach the knockout stage. And with testing-looking trips to Milan and Anderlecht still to come, their progress is far from certain.

Europe has arrived – but it can also wait. Sunderland’s priority has to be preserving their Premier League status, not least given what a slog it was for them to get back to this level in the first place (eight years outside the top flight, including four languishing in the third tier). But while they are undeniably in a relegation battle as things stand, there’s no reason to think they’re doomed.

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...
