#925. ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA’s chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 44-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4bn) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the players’ union for England and Wales observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event – and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. It’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

Then there is the question of integrity. Summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer , establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says. “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “We live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on,” he says. “They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people who have a good product. We need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

#923. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#922. Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

#921. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#920. Swing when you’re winning? Biggest leaps across Fifa’s football rankings | The Knowledge

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”

The gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

It is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data shows it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”

Some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”

That 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

That is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

Pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

“The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”

“Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

It is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

Those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

The answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

“Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

“It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”

Chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

Milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the new champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”

“Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

“Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

“My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.

#919. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

To find out what other jobs you could have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#918. Wiegman cites young talent as key to new England deal after calling up Goodwin

Head coach excited by ‘high potential’ of players

Striker Goodwin and keeper Cox in squad for first time

Sarina Wiegman says the potential in England’s emerging young players helped convince her to extend her contract until the end of 2029’s European Championship.

The Lionesses head coach, whose previous deal was due to expire next year, gave first senior call-ups to the striker Isobel Goodwin and goalkeeper Katie Cox on Tuesday as she named her squad for December’s two-leg World Cup qualifying playoff against Ukraine.

Speaking to the media for the first time since she signed her new contract in October, Wiegman described the Football Association as “a trailblazer with the women’s game and a great federation to work for” and said: “I’m really happy with the team but also talents coming through, which is exciting, and there’s now some high potential, and hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players, if not already. And I hope to have a part in that, too, and have a contribution to that. While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited.

“The majority of their development is happening [at their clubs] but when they come to our environment, I hope to have a little part of that contribution.”

The Dutchwoman has led England to three consecutive major tournament finals, lifting two European titles, since taking charge in 2021 on a deal to 2025. Asked whether she had expected that to become an eight-year stay, she said: “No. I thought: ‘Four years, that’s a long time.’ Then it became six years and that looks like it’s becoming eight years. I would never have expected all of the things that we have reached.”

Will she call it a day in 2029? “Well, I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know! I don’t plan that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”

Goalkeepers: Katie Cox (Nottingham Forest on loan from Chelsea), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool)Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Taylor Hinds (Arsenal), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Poppy Pattinson (London City Lionesses), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Grace Clinton (Manchester City), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Ella Toone (Manchester United), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)Forwards: Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea), Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Isobel Goodwin (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal)

Wiegman, whose latest 25-player squad includes 10 players with fewer than 10 caps, watched from the stands at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday as Goodwin scored for London City Lionesses with a terrific finish against Arsenal. She said of the 23-year-old: “We always knew she’s a huge talent [with] a high potential. We’re watching a lot of games over periods of time, all the time, so we [had] kept an eye on her anyway, but I think it also helped that she had that great goal and a great performance last Sunday.

“She has some different qualities. She’s really fast too. She can head – she showed that also in attacking set plays and defending set plays also – and she can score goals. Does she need to step up to the next level? Absolutely. But you can tell that she’s improving.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Wiegman was unable to call upon several injured players, including Lauren James and Alex Greenwood. She included Manchester United’s Ella Toone, who was initially left out of September’s squad before being recalled for the playoff against Greece. Wiegman said of Toone: “She has impressed us really well. She responded really well. And going back to [her] club, she’s done well too. And that’s what has been fed back to me too.”

Cox is rare in getting an England call-up while playing in the second-tier WSL2. The 20-year-old is on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea.

The Lionesses face Ukraine on neutral territory in Spain in the away leg on 1 December before playing them at Wembley four days later.

#917. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#914. Portugal’s new No 7 Forbs channels Ronaldo for winner as Wales are denied

One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese Football Federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.

For Wales, a Nations League relegation playoff double-header awaits in March, with Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia and Herzegovina – who knocked them out of World Cup qualifying this year – all potential opponents in Friday’s draw in Switzerland. Afterwards Craig Bellamy stressed the importance of keeping elite company to accelerate improvement but reiterated that he will not be in the job beyond Euro 2028, after which his contract expires.

“If we want to develop as a ­football nation and continue to move ­forward, we have to be playing against the best teams,” Bellamy said. “It’s only going to improve us. I was the best manager going in [Group] B, finished top … how good am I? Now I’m in [Group] A, we’ve played quite well, but I’m crap. It’s about playing the best teams, that’s how we’re going to get better. I won’t be here for the next Nations League, I won’t be the manager then, so I’m doing it for the next one.”

This was a welcome victory for ­Portugal, who advanced to the quarter-finals as group winners after a bruising 4-1 home defeat by Denmark in Braga. Turn a new page and all that. There were plenty of positive takeaways for Wales too. David Brooks cancelled out Bruno Fernandes’s opener and Wales seized the lead through Sorba Thomas, who applied the ­finish after a slick team move. But Neto, who picked up two bookings inside two minutes, the second for a foul on Brennan Johnson, levelled before half-time. Bellamy’s side were fun and, at times, freewheeling but Forbs had the final say with a neat run and finish.

Bellamy stressed the importance of locking down Vitinha and João Neves, two of his favourite players, but Wales did not allow the Paris Saint-Germain pair to have things all their own way. It was a ludicrously open game and, approaching the half-time interval at 2-2, a stray Renato Veiga pass supplied the all-action Harry Wilson with a speculative opportunity from halfway. Wilson intercepted the ball and, after taking a touch to roll it into the opposition half, the Leeds midfielder launched a marvellous left-foot lobbed effort towards goal, his 45-yard shot skimming the roof of Diogo Costa’s goal net.

Portugal may have levelled a few moments earlier, Neto easily beating Jay Dasilva in the six-yard box to prod in Francisco Trincão’s brilliant cross, but Wilson’s attempt at the audacious was another gentle reminder of Portugal’s precarious state. After suffering their heaviest competitive home defeat against Denmark on Saturday, Portugal were again susceptible defensively. Before Thomas capped a scintillating team move to seize the lead on 40 minutes, Wilson twice went close, Diogo Dalot making a desperate block for the first.

This was an entertaining contest for which it was worth braving the winter conditions. When Fernandes picked his spot on 11 minutes, sending an unerring strike into the top corner, Portugal appeared in the groove. But Wales responded two minutes later when Brooks, who scored with a superb dinked finish in Norway, dug out another clever effort. Wilson saw a shot repelled by Costa but when the ball squirted free Rubin Colwill had the presence of mind to calmly square for Brooks, who squeezed a left-foot shot into the far corner. Colwill, a fan favourite here for Cardiff, thoroughly enjoyed his first Wales start under Bellamy.

Colwill impressed in a deep midfield role alongside Josh Sheehan of Bolton, whose former clubmate Aaron Collins, now of MK Dons, arrived from the bench midway through the second half for his debut. Portugal, meanwhile, introduced João Félix and the Club Brugge winger Forbs, the latter wearing the tweaked No 7 shirt that will always be ­synonymous with Ronaldo. An unmarked Ben Cabango, who replaced Joe Rodon as a precaution at half-time, went close to earning Wales the lead with a header. The weary look on Costa’s face as he pawed Cabango’s header away from goal for a corner said it all.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The moment Forbs surged on to a loose Cabango header and then at Davies before applying a low finish provided light relief on an uncomfortable night. For Wales, a challenging campaign ended as it began, with a heartening defeat by Portugal.

“Look, it’s a £1.2bn squad against a £170m squad,” Bellamy said. “I live in the real world. I’m beyond happy. I couldn’t ask for more. Against a top team, if you make a couple of mistakes as we did, you will get punished. We’ve offered a really good version of ourselves, we’ve been a massive part of this group. It’s just about those fine margins.”

#913. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#912. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

#911. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#909. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#908. Nations League roundup: Devenny’s divine strike lifts Northern Ireland to top tier

Haaland’s late penalty grabs Norway last-eight spot

Parrott penalties help Republic of Ireland secure playoff

A wonder strike from Justin Devenny earned Northern Ireland top spot in Nations League Group B2 and promotion to the top tier of the competition. The Stoke player fired home on the volley from the edge of the area to earn a 1-1 draw away to Hungary, who would have leapfrogged Michael O’Neill’s side in the group with victory.

Northern Ireland had fallen 1-0 behind after a 35th-minute goal from the striker Barnabas Varga, who slotted home when one-on-one with the goalkeeper Pierce Charles after a defensive mix-up. The goal ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign and also sent Hungary to the top of the group in the live standings.

But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for O’Neill’s young outfit, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders. As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation – with Rajmund Toth firing over late on – but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of their campaign.

“It’s a great feeling for us,” said O’Neill, who had to watch the game from the stands as he served a touchline ban. “We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.

“We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 [qualification] but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we’ve given against some very good teams, it’s very encouraging.”

In Wales’s group, Norway snatched a quarter-final berth thanks to Erling Haaland’s 96th-minute penalty against Denmark. It was Haaland’s second and completed a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down as the Danes were pipped for second place in Group A4.

Denmark, who began the day in second place in the standings and needed to avoid defeat to reach the knockout phase, led 2-0 inside 14 minutes through Rasmus Højlund and Pierre-Emile Højbjerg.

But Haaland pulled one back before half-time and, after Martin Ødegaard’s 83rd-minute equaliser had set up a grandstand finish, the Manchester City striker scored from the spot in the sixth minute of added time after the video assistant referee had ruled Joachim Andersen had handled in the area.

The two nations finished level on nine points and although Denmark had a better goal difference, Norway progressed on their head-to-head record after also winning the reverse fixture 3-2.

“It’s one of the crazier football years,” Haaland told TV2. “It’s fun to be a part of finishing it off in style. Ståle [Solbakken, Norway’s coach] said ⁠it before the match: ‘Let’s just get a good finish now to a completely indescribable football year.’ It’s fun to be Norwegian.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Norway’s latest success came ​on the back of their memorable World Cup run, when Haaland ‌and Ødegaard led the country to the ‌quarter-finals in their first appearance at the tournament for 28 years. “It’s completely fantastic and fun,” Haaland said. “I should have had a hat-trick today, ‌but I’m happy with two goals, so that’s totally fine.”

The Republic of Ireland beat 10-man Kosovo 3-0 at the Aviva Stadium to go ahead of the visitors in the standings for Group B3 to secure second place and a spot in the promotion playoffs. The win also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month’s qualifying draw for that competition.

Kreshnik Hajrizi’s first-half handball on the line earned the Kosovo defender a red card and allowed Troy Parrott to bury the resulting penalty. The Republic were awarded a second spot-kick early in the second period after a foul by the goalkeeper Arijanet Muric, with Parrott again scoring. Jack Moylan’s header from a Liam Kitching cross made it 3-0.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, the red card incident sparked by Moylan’s cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott. His effort – clearly goalbound – was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately sent off.
